content.title: About
content.content: Carrot is a root vegetable belonging to the Apiaceae family, widely cultivated worldwide. It has a sweet taste, crisp texture, and bright orange color due to its high beta‑carotene content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrots are technically biennial plants, but are cultivated as annuals for their edible roots.
The orange color was developed through Dutch breeding in the 17th century.
There are over 100 carrot varieties, including purple, yellow, red, and white.
Beta‑carotene in carrots is converted to vitamin A in the body, essential for vision.
Carrots can grow in low‑nitrogen soils but require good drainage.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is a precursor of vitamin A, supporting eye health and immunity.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Fiber and potassium help lower blood pressure.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lycopene and other carotenoids combat free radicals.

items.title: Helps regulate blood sugar
items.content: Low glycemic index and fiber promote gradual glucose rise.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Fiber improves intestinal motility and prevents constipation.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to carrots.

items.title: Excess vitamin A
items.content: Very high consumption can lead to hypervitaminosis A, causing skin yellowing.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet varieties may be a concern for those monitoring sugar intake.

items.title: Soil contamination
items.content: Carrots can accumulate heavy metals from polluted soils, so source them responsibly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Carrots can be eaten raw as sticks, added to salads, soups, stews, roasted, steamed, or used in baking. Grated carrot is common in desserts and carrot cakes. Carrot juice is a popular refreshing drink.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store carrots in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, preferably in a perforated bag or a container with a small amount of water. In a cool, dark place they can keep for several weeks. Keep carrots away from ethylene‑producing fruits, as they accelerate spoilage.
